selection.rule: Twenty artworks from the coverage set's CORE (research/v3/data/coverage-set/coverage-set-1.json, role === 'core'), which is the canonical tuning bench; NOT from eval-142, which COVERAGE_SET.md establishes was never a sample of this corpus. Two steps, neither of which looks at any model answer. (1) PINNED: every core artwork the group-BCDE pilot actually decoded — there are three, and they are the only artworks in the whole core where a reviewer-vs-E/F comparison is possible at all, so all three are taken. (2) DRAWN: the remaining slots, apportioned across the core's own resolution tiers in proportion to the core's tier mix (largest remainder, ties to the larger tier), and inside each tier taken by a seeded round-robin over clusters — every cluster is visited at most once before any is revisited, so twenty artworks land in twenty different clusters wherever the tier quotas allow. Seed 20260803. Deliberately NOT re-selected on E-vs-F disagreement (§3's rule, restated by §15.9): a round conditioned on disagreement is a different population and must be reported as one. WORDING: every stem and every gloss is parsed byte-identically out of variant E's prompt file (the "N. " enumerator is the only thing dropped, because this round has eight passes and not thirteen). §15.9: E and F word the same questions differently, so scoring F against these answers carries a stated wording caveat that scoring E does not. THE JOIN: only 2 of the 200 core artworks were decoded by the pilot on the same bytes, and 1 more at another rendition — so on the other artworks in this round there is no model answer to compare against yet, and the round's product there is a reviewer label on the coverage set and an answer to 'is this question answerable by a human at all'.

questions.question: texture_noise - is there visible grain or noise over large parts of the cover?
questions.instruction: Answer this one question only. Do not try to make your answers across questions tell one story.
questions.preamble:
WHAT COUNTS AS TEXT. Any lettering you can read as letters or words, anywhere on the cover: the title, the artist name, small print, the wordmark inside a logo, and writing that belongs to a photographed scene such as a shop sign or a slogan on a shirt.

WHAT COUNTS AS ADDED ON. Some things sit on top of a cover without being part of the picture: a parental advisory sticker, a record label's logo, a barcode or a price tag, a watermark from a shop or a stock library. The test is who put it there, not how it looks. A record label logo can be a kind of text and an added-on element at the same time; two different questions ask about it and they are not rivals.

THE MAIN SUBJECT. The thing the cover is of: a person, a face, an animal, an object, a vehicle, a building. Lettering is not a subject. A pattern is not a subject. When there is more than one, take them all together — except where a single kind of thing is asked for, and then name the kind of the largest one.

ONE PICTURE, ONE MEDIUM. If more than one way of making a picture is present, name the one that makes up most of the cover. A photograph with lettering over it is a photograph. Lettering on a plain field, with no picture at all, is typography_only.

THE SIGNATURE COLOUR. One colour a person would name if you asked them what colour that cover is. Not the colour that covers the most area, and not a colour you have to hunt for. Plenty of covers do not have one, and no is a real answer.

LISTS. Two of the thirteen questions take a list instead of one answer. List every value that applies and list each value only once.

MEASURING. Do not work out colours, contrast or exact sizes. Where a size or a range is asked for, a rough eyeball is what is wanted.

ANSWERING. Answer each question on its own. Do not try to make your answers tell one story.

answers.label: yes
answers.gloss: film grain, print dots, sensor noise, or added speckle, over a large area

answers.label: no
answers.gloss: the surfaces are clean
